summary: Entity Attestation Tokens carry evidence about a device in remote attestation (RATS). When they are sent in places like REST APIs they need media types. This memo defines media types for EATs.

eli5.summary: Computers label what is inside a package so the receiver knows how to open it. This creates those labels for device "trust report" packages.

questions: what is an entity attestation token
subtitle: Six registered media types that label Entity Attestation Tokens when they travel over HTTP, CoAP and similar protocols.

tldr.problem: Remote attestation messages carry Entity Attestation Tokens (EATs), but APIs need a media type to label the payload, and EAT has six wire formats.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9782 registers six media types, one per EAT wire format, each with an optional eat_profile parameter that mirrors the profile claim inside the token. It also registers the +cwt structured syntax suffix and six CoAP Content-Format numbers.
tldr.outcome: Protocol and API designers get ready-made media types for EAT-based messages, with the profile visible at the API layer. The media type is only a clue: receivers must still check the data.

today: RFC 9782 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on RFC 9711 and RFC 9781.

sections.title: Why EATs Need Media Types
sections.content:
In Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS), an Attester produces evidence about itself, a Verifier appraises it, and a Relying Party uses the result. The RFC's first figure shows these messages carried in a REST API: the Attester sends POST /verify with an EAT holding Evidence, the Verifier answers 200 OK with an EAT holding Attestation Results, and the Attester then sends POST /auth to the Relying Party, which replies 201 Created.

This memo defines media types for EAT payloads independently of which RATS conceptual message they carry. The aim is to give protocol, API and application designers reusable media types for HTTP or the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP). It relies on the terms in the RATS architecture, RFC 9334.
sections.eli5: Devices send each other reports about whether they can be trusted. Each report needs a clear label on the outside, so whoever gets it knows what kind of report it is.

sections.title: The Six EAT Wire Formats
sections.content:
RFC 9782 describes six EAT wire formats and how they relate. RFC 9711 defines four: the CBOR Web Token (CWT), the JSON Web Token (JWT), and the detached EAT bundle in its JSON and CBOR flavours. RFC 9781 defines the other two: the Unprotected CWT Claims Set (UCCS) and the Unprotected JWT Claims Set (UJCS).

Each format gets its own media type. The CWT and JWT forms are the protected ones, the bundle types carry detached EATs, and the two ucs types carry claims sets that are not protected by the token itself.
sections.eli5: There are six kinds of envelope for these reports: some are sealed with a signature, some are not, and some hold several reports at once. Each kind gets its own label.

sections.title: The eat_profile Parameter
sections.content:
EAT is open and flexible, so RFC 9711 defines EAT profiles that pin down what producers and consumers must understand: which claims, which serialisation, which signature schemes and so on. A token names its profile in-band with the eat_profile claim, whose value is either an OID or a URI.

Every media type here accepts an optional eat_profile parameter that mirrors that claim. Exposing the profile at the API layer lets API routers send a payload straight to the right profile-specific processor without looking inside the request body. The expectation is that a profile automatically gets a more specific media type derived from the base one, such as application/eat+cwt.

In HTTP, an absolute URI value uses the quoted-string encoding. An OID may use the plain token encoding, without quotes. The registrations add that OIDs must use dotted-decimal notation and that the parameter value is case insensitive.
sections.eli5: On top of the label you can add a note saying exactly which rulebook the report follows. A mail sorter can read the note and send the package to the right desk without opening it.

sections.title: Example Verification Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC gives a REST verification example. The request is a POST to /challenge-response/v1/session/1234567890 on verifier.example. Its Content-Type is application/eat+cwt with the profile tag:evidence.example,2022, and its Accept header asks for application/eat+cwt with the profile tag:ar4si.example,2021.

The response is 200 OK with that same media type and profile. In both messages a tag URI identifies the profile as an explicit parameter, so the sender transports evidence and also negotiates the acceptable format of the result.
sections.eli5: You hand over your report and say, "I would like the answer written in this style." The reply comes back labelled in exactly that style.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Media types only provide clues to the processing application. The application must verify that the received data matches the expected format regardless of the advertised media type, and stop processing if it does not. Skipping this could expose the user to risks such as privilege escalation and cross-protocol attacks.

The security considerations of RFC 9711 and RFC 9781 apply in full. For application/eat-ucs+json and application/eat-ucs+cbor in particular, readers should review Section 3 of RFC 9781, which discusses the characteristics of a secure channel for conveying such messages.
sections.eli5: A label on a box can be wrong. Always look inside and check it matches before you use it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered the +cwt structured syntax suffix, meaning the media type is encoded as a CWT (RFC 8392). The change controller is the RATS Working Group and the IETF has change control.

IANA has also registered six media types: application/eat+cwt, application/eat+jwt, application/eat-bun+cbor, application/eat-bun+json, application/eat-ucs+cbor and application/eat-ucs+json. All have an optional eat_profile parameter, intended usage COMMON and no restrictions on usage. They are meant for Attesters, Verifiers, Endorsers, Reference-Value providers and Relying Parties moving EAT payloads over HTTP(S), CoAP(S) and other transports.

Finally, six CoAP Content-Format numbers, 263 to 268, map to the same types in the same order.
sections.eli5: The official list of labels now has six new entries, and the small-device messaging system has six matching short numbers.
